notes.variety: Standard written Khasi, the Sohra (Cherrapunji) dialect that Khasi textbooks and the Bible translation use, in the everyday spoken form heard in Shillong. Address is shown with phi (polite and plural) first, and me/pha (informal singular, male/female listener) where a chunk changes. English loanwords that every Shillong speaker uses (bas, tiket, ophis, phone) are kept as they are said.
notes.turns: Khasi verbs never change shape; time and aspect are carried by short particles in front of the verb. la marks past (nga la leit, I went), yn marks future and fuses with the pronoun (ngan leit, I will go), sa adds 'later' (ngan sa leit). dang before a verb means 'in the middle of' and covers every progressive cell (nga dang bam, I am eating; nga la dang bam, I was eating). lah before a verb means 'already, completed' and does the work of the perfect (nga lah bam, I have eaten; nga la lah bam, I had eaten). ju marks habit (nga ju leit, I usually go; nga la ju leit, I used to go). There is no separate conditional or subjunctive: lada (if) plus the same particles covers the first conditional, and lada ... la ... with yn la in the main clause covers the counterfactual ones. Negation is ym, fused to the pronoun (ngam, phim, um, kam), with shym added for the past (ngam shym la leit).
notes.wordOrder: Basic order is subject, verb, object, like English, but the subject is always echoed by its gender marker: u Bah u leit (Bah, he goes), ka kmie ka bam. Direct and indirect objects that are people or definite things take ïa in front of them (nga ïohi ïa u, I see him). Particles stack in a fixed order before the verb: negation, then la/yn, then dang/lah/ju, then the verb (ngam la dang bam). Connectors never change word order: lada, namar ba, haba, wat la all sit at the front of their clause and the clause stays subject-verb-object. Questions keep statement order; a yes/no question rises at the end or takes the tag ne em, and question words (aiu, mano, hangno, lano, kumno) usually stand at the front but can also stay in place.
notes.slotGrammar: The heart of Khasi is the four markers u (masculine), ka (feminine), i (small, dear, or neutral) and ki (plural): every noun carries one, and the same marker returns as the subject echo, the pronoun and the relative marker (u briew uba wan, the man who comes). There is no a/the distinction: ka ïing is both 'a house' and 'the house', and the plural is simply ki ïing. Nouns have no case; roles are shown by ïa (object), jong (of, possession), ha/sha/na (at, to, from) and bad (with). Adjectives follow the noun and take the noun's marker again (ka ïing kaba heh, a house that is big). Numbers need a classifier: ngut for people (ar ngut ki briew), tylli for things (lai tylli ki kot).
notes.sound: ñ is the palatal nasal of Spanish señor (khlaiñ, kñi) and ï is a y-glide (ïa, ïing) that English speakers wrongly read as a vowel. Aspirated kh, th, ph contrast with plain k, t, p and change meaning (ka, the; kha, to be born), so the puff of air must be audible. y between consonants is a short schwa (kynthei, pyrthei, syiem), not the English 'ee' or 'eye'. Final p, t, k are unreleased, and initial ng (nga, ngi, ngut) starts a word with the sound at the end of English 'sing'. Stress falls on the last syllable of the root, so prefixes jing-, pyn-, nong- stay unstressed: jingBAM, nongTREI.
notes.register: phi is the safe 'you' for everyone: strangers, elders, groups, and anyone you would call Bah or Kong. me (to a male) and pha (to a female) are for close friends, children, and younger relatives, and sound rude to anyone else. Chunks shift by swapping the pronoun (Phi long kumno? / Me long kumno?) and by adding sngewbha (please) or the softening imperative particle To; elders are addressed with kinship titles (Bah, Kong, Mei, Pa) rather than by name.

turnGrid.note: la before the verb is the whole past tense; the verb leit never changes. Negative: ngam shym la leit.
la (past) plus dang (in the middle of). In a story the la is often dropped once the past is set: nga dang leit haba ...
la plus lah (already, completed). Usually paired with shwa ba (before) to mark the earlier of two past events.
Bare verb: habit, fact, and also the present moment when dang is not needed. man ka sngi (every day) makes the habit explicit.
dang means 'still, in the middle of'. It is the only progressive marker and is used far less than the English -ing form.
lah alone before a verb means 'already done'. Experience ('have you ever') uses la ju: phi la ju leit? Not yet: ngam pat leit.
yn fuses with the pronoun: ngan, phin, un, kan, ngin, kin. sa adds 'later': ngan sa leit. Negative: ngan ym leit.
yn plus dang. Rare; Khasi normally just says ngan leit with a time word (lashai, mynstep).
yn plus lah. For 'finished by' add dep after the verb and haduh (by): ngan lah trei dep haduh janmiet.

items.target: Khublei, phi long kumno? / Khublei, leit suk
items.gloss: Hello, how are you? / Goodbye, go well

example.target: Khublei, Kong! Phi long kumno? — Nga khlaiñ, khublei. Bad phi?
example.gloss: Hello, Kong! How are you? — I'm well, thanks. And you?

items.note: Uses C-HELLO-BYE. Khublei is hello, thanks and goodbye at once; the leaving person says shong suk (stay well), the one staying says leit suk (go well).

items.target: Ka kyrteng jong nga ka long ___ / Nga wan na ___ / Nga dei u/ka ___
items.gloss: My name is ___ / I come from ___ / I am a ___

example.target: Ka kyrteng jong nga ka long Arjun. Nga wan na Shillong bad nga dei u nonghikai.
example.gloss: My name is Arjun. I come from Shillong and I am a teacher.

items.note: Uses C-MY-NAME, D-BE, G-FROM. Pick u or ka for yourself: nga dei u nonghikai (a man), nga dei ka nonghikai (a woman).

items.target: Khublei shibun / Khublei, ym don eiei
items.gloss: Thank you very much / Thanks (in reply), it is nothing

example.target: Khublei shibun, Bah. — Khublei, ym don eiei.
example.gloss: Thank you very much, Bah. — You're welcome, it's nothing.

items.note: Uses C-PLEASE-THANKS. The reply to thanks is simply Khublei again; ym don eiei (there is nothing) is the 'no problem' add-on.

items.target: Katno ka dor jong kane? / Katno kane?
items.gloss: How much is the price of this? / How much is this?

example.target: Katno ka dor jong kane ka jainsem? — Ka long lai spah tyngka.
example.gloss: How much is this jainsem? — It's three hundred rupees.

items.note: Uses C-HOW-MUCH and S-NUMBERS. Katno is 'how much' for prices and amounts; the answer uses ka long plus a number and tyngka (rupees).

items.target: Hangno ka ___? / Ka don hangno? / Leit beit, sha kti mon
items.gloss: Where is the ___? / Where is it? / Go straight, to the right

example.target: Map, hangno ka bas stand? — Leit beit, hadien kata, sha kti mon.
example.gloss: Excuse me, where is the bus stand? — Go straight, after that, turn right.

items.note: Uses C-WHERE-IS and D-THERE-IS. hangno asks for a location, shano for a direction (Shano phi leit? Where are you going?). kti mon is right, kti diang is left.

items.target: Ngam sngewthuh / Sngewbha ong biang / Kren kham suki, sngewbha
items.gloss: I don't understand / Please say it again / Speak more slowly, please

example.target: Map, ngam sngewthuh. Sngewbha kren kham suki.
example.gloss: Sorry, I don't understand. Please speak more slowly.

items.note: Uses C-DONT-UNDERSTAND and C-REPEAT-PLEASE. sngewthuh is 'understand'; the negative fuses ym into the pronoun: ngam. suki is slow, kham makes it 'more'.

items.target: Nga ieid ïa ___ / Ngam ieid ïa ___
items.gloss: I like ___ / I don't like ___

example.target: Nga ieid shibun ïa ka jadoh, hynrei ngam ieid ïa ka tungrymbai.
example.gloss: I really like jadoh, but I don't like tungrymbai.

items.note: Uses D-LIKE, G-BUT, T-NEG. ieid covers both like and love; the liked thing takes ïa. sngewtynnad ban (enjoy doing) works before a verb.

items.target: Nga kwah ___ / Ai ïa nga ___, sngewbha
items.gloss: I want ___ / Give me ___, please

example.target: Ai ïa nga ka sha kawei bad ka jadoh kawei, sngewbha.
example.gloss: Give me one tea and one jadoh, please.

items.note: Uses D-WANT, D-WOULD-LIKE, C-PLEASE-THANKS. Ordering is done with the imperative ai (give) plus sngewbha; kawei/uwei (one) after the noun counts it.

items.target: nga dei u/ka ___ / nga long ___
items.gloss: I am a ___ (identity) / I am ___ (state, origin)

example.target: Nga dei u Khasi. Nga long u nongpule ha Shillong.
example.gloss: I am a Khasi. I am a student in Shillong.

items.note: dei is 'be' for identity and correctness, long for state, becoming and origin. The noun after dei needs its own marker: nga dei u doktor, not nga dei doktor.

items.target: nga don ___
items.gloss: I have ___

example.target: Nga don ar ngut ki para bad ka ksew kawei.
example.gloss: I have two siblings and one dog.

items.note: don means both 'have' and 'there is'; the subject decides which. Age also uses don: nga don arphew snem (I am twenty). Negative: ngam don.

items.target: don ___ / ha ___ don ___
items.gloss: there is ___ / in ___ there is ___

example.target: Ha Shillong don bun ki dukan bad ki ïing bam.
example.gloss: In Shillong there are many shops and restaurants.

items.note: Same verb as D-HAVE, with no subject pronoun: Don ka ïew hangne? (Is there a market here?). The noun keeps its ka/ki marker.

items.target: nga ieid ïa ___ / nga sngewtynnad ban ___
items.gloss: I like ___ / I enjoy ___-ing

example.target: Nga ieid ïa ka jingrwai Khasi bad nga sngewtynnad ban rwai.
example.gloss: I like Khasi music and I enjoy singing.

items.note: ieid takes ïa before the liked noun; sngewtynnad takes ban before a verb. Learners drop the ïa: nga ieid ka sha is wrong, nga ieid ïa ka sha is right.

items.target: nga kwah ___ / nga kwah ban ___
items.gloss: I want ___ / I want to ___

example.target: Nga kwah ban nang ka ktien Khasi mynta u snem.
example.gloss: I want to learn Khasi this year.

items.note: A noun follows kwah directly (nga kwah ka sha); a verb needs ban in between. ban is the all-purpose 'to' before a second verb.

items.target: nga kwah ban ___, sngewbha / ai ïa nga ___, sngewbha
items.gloss: I'd like to ___, please / please give me ___

example.target: Ai ïa nga ka kophi kawei, sngewbha.
example.gloss: I'd like a coffee, please.

items.note: Khasi has no conditional 'would'; politeness comes from sngewbha (please) and from the tone. In a shop ai ïa nga (give me) plus sngewbha is normal, not blunt.

items.target: nga donkam ïa ___ / nga donkam ban ___
items.gloss: I need ___ / I need to ___

example.target: Nga donkam ban thied ka tiket shwa ban leit sha Sohra.
example.gloss: I need to buy a ticket before going to Sohra.

items.note: donkam takes ïa before a noun and ban before a verb. hap ban means 'have to, be obliged to' and is stronger; don't mix them up.

items.target: nga lah ban ___
items.gloss: I can ___

example.target: Nga lah ban kren khyndiat ka ktien Khasi.
example.gloss: I can speak a little Khasi.

items.note: lah ban plus verb is ability and permission. Without ban, lah means 'already, finished' (nga lah bam, I have eaten), so the ban is load-bearing.

items.target: ngan sa ___ / nga la thmu ban ___
items.gloss: I'm going to ___ (later) / I have planned to ___

example.target: Ngan sa leit sha Sohra bad ki lok jong nga.
example.gloss: I'm going to go to Sohra with my friends.

items.note: yn (future) fuses with the pronoun: ngan, phin, un, kan, ngin, kin. sa adds 'later, next'; thmu ban (plan to) makes the intention explicit.

items.target: ngan ___ / ngan ym ___
items.gloss: I will ___ / I won't ___

example.target: Ngan wan biang lashai mynstep.
example.gloss: I will come back tomorrow morning.

items.note: The future is the same yn particle as D-GOING-TO; Khasi does not split will from going to. Negative future: ngan ym wan (I won't come).

items.target: pronoun + verb (nga bam, u bam, ki bam)
items.gloss: present simple: bare verb

example.target: Man ka sngi nga dih ka sha mynstep.
example.gloss: Every day I drink tea in the morning.

items.note: No endings, no agreement: bam is bam for every person. Add man ka sngi (every day) or mynta (now) to fix the meaning when it matters.

items.target: pronoun + dang + verb
items.gloss: present continuous: dang before the verb

example.target: Nga dang trei mynta, ngan sa kren bad phi hadien.
example.gloss: I'm working right now, I'll talk with you later.

items.note: dang is 'still, in the middle of'. It is used for genuinely ongoing actions; habits and states take the bare verb, never dang.

items.target: pronoun + la + verb (nga la leit, nga la bam, nga la don)
items.gloss: past simple: la before the verb

example.target: Mynhynnin nga la leit sha ïew bad nga la thied ka jhur.
example.gloss: Yesterday I went to the market and bought vegetables.

items.note: One particle does all past tenses: la leit (went), la don (had), la long (was). Once la is set in a story it can be dropped on later verbs.

items.target: pronoun + yn (fused) + verb: ngan, phin, un, kan, ngin, kin
items.gloss: future: yn fused to the pronoun

example.target: Lashai ngin leit sha Sohra, kan slap ne em?
example.gloss: Tomorrow we'll go to Sohra, will it rain or not?

items.note: Write the fused forms as one word (ngan, un, kan); older texts write nga'n. ym in the future sits after the fused pronoun: ngan ym leit.

items.target: ym fused: ngam, phim, um, kam, ngim, kim / past: ngam shym la ___
items.gloss: not: ym fused to the pronoun; shym added in the past

example.target: Ngam tip. Ngam shym la ïohi ïa u mynhynnin.
example.gloss: I don't know. I didn't see him yesterday.

items.note: ym fuses into the pronoun and comes before every other particle: ngam dang bam (I'm not eating). Past negatives add shym: ngam shym la leit.

items.target: statement + rising tone / ___ ne em? / Hato ___?
items.gloss: yes/no question: intonation, the tag ne em, or Hato

example.target: Phi lah bam? — Hooid, nga lah bam. — Phi kwah ka sha ne em?
example.gloss: Have you eaten? — Yes, I've eaten. — Do you want tea or not?

items.note: Word order never changes for questions. ne em (or not) is the everyday tag; Hato at the front is bookish. Answers: hooid (yes), em (no).

items.target: aiu (what), mano (who), hangno/shano (where), lano (when), kumno (how), katno (how much), balei (why)
items.gloss: wh-words

example.target: Shano phi leit? Aiu phi bam? Balei phi la wan lait?
example.gloss: Where are you going? What are you eating? Why did you come late?

items.note: The question word usually opens the sentence and the rest stays in statement order. hangno is 'where at', shano 'where to'; lano is 'when'.

example.target: Nga bam ka ja bad ka jhur, bad nga dih ka sha.
example.gloss: I eat rice and vegetables, and I drink tea.

items.note: bad joins nouns and clauses and also means 'with'. Two subjects each keep their marker: u kpa bad ka kmie ki wan (father and mother, they come).

items.target: ___, hynrei ___

example.target: Nga kwah ban wan, hynrei nga hap ban trei.
example.gloss: I want to come, but I have to work.

items.note: hynrei is the everyday 'but' and also 'however' at sentence start. No word-order change follows it.

example.target: Phi kwah ka sha ne ka kophi?
example.gloss: Do you want tea or coffee?

items.note: ne is the plain 'or'; lane is 'or else, alternatively'. ne em at the end of a sentence is the yes/no tag 'or not'.

items.target: ___ namar ba ___ / namar ka ___
items.gloss: ___ because ___ / because of the ___

example.target: Ngam lah ban wan namar ba nga dang pang.
example.gloss: I can't come because I'm ill.

items.note: namar ba before a clause, namar alone before a noun (namar ka slap, because of the rain). The clause after it stays in normal order.

items.target: hadien kata, ___ / te ___
items.gloss: after that, ___ / then ___

example.target: Nga la bam mynstep, hadien kata nga la leit sha skul.
example.gloss: I ate in the morning, after that I went to school.

items.note: hadien kata (after that) opens the next step; te is a light 'then, so' that hangs on the end of the first clause: nga la bam te nga la leit.

items.target: ___ ruh
items.gloss: ___ also / too (after the word it stresses)

example.target: Nga ruh nga wan na Shillong.
example.gloss: I too come from Shillong.

items.note: ruh follows the word it belongs to, never precedes it: nga ruh (me too), kane ruh (this too). It also makes 'even': wat u ruh (even he).

items.target: ha ___ (place) / ha u bnai ___ (month) / hapoh ___ (inside)
items.gloss: in ___

example.target: Nga shong ha Shillong; nga la kha ha u bnai Mei.
example.gloss: I live in Shillong; I was born in May.

items.note: ha is the general 'at, in, on' for location and time. hapoh is the physical 'inside'. Months take u bnai plus the English name.

items.target: ha ___ / halor ___ (on top of)
items.gloss: on ___

example.target: Ka kot ka don halor ka miej. Ngin ïakynduh ha ka sngi Sunday.
example.gloss: The book is on the table. We'll meet on Sunday.

items.note: For a surface use halor (on top of); for days and dates plain ha is enough (ha ka sngi Sunday). English 'on' has no single Khasi word.

items.target: ha ___ (place) / ha ___ baje (o'clock)
items.gloss: at ___

example.target: Ngin ïakynduh ha ka ïing bam ha san baje janmiet.
example.gloss: We'll meet at the restaurant at five in the evening.

items.note: Clock times are number plus baje: san baje (five o'clock), shiphew baje (ten). ha before the time is optional in speech.

items.target: na ___
items.gloss: from ___

example.target: Nga wan na Meghalaya, na ka shnong Sohra.
example.gloss: I come from Meghalaya, from the village of Sohra.

items.note: na is 'from' for origin and source; naduh is 'since, starting from' a time (naduh mynhynnin). ïoh na (get from) uses the same word.

items.target: sha ___
items.gloss: to ___ (direction, towards)

example.target: Ngan leit sha ïew, hadien kata sha ïing.
example.gloss: I'll go to the market, after that home.

items.note: sha marks direction, ha marks location: leit sha ïew (go to market) but don ha ïew (be at the market). Never use sha for giving; that is ïa.

items.target: bad ___ / lem bad ___
items.gloss: with ___ / together with ___

example.target: Ngan leit sha Sohra lem bad ki lok jong nga.
example.gloss: I'll go to Sohra together with my friends.

items.note: bad is 'and' and 'with' at once; lem bad makes the 'together with' reading explicit. Instruments use da: kut da ka tari (cut with a knife).

items.target: nga, me (m.) / pha (f.) / phi (polite, pl.), u, ka, i, ngi, ki
items.gloss: I, you, he, she, it, we, they

example.target: Nga dei u Khasi; phi dei ka Bengali; u long u lok jong nga.
example.gloss: I am Khasi; you are Bengali; he is my friend.

items.note: The gender markers double as pronouns: u is 'he' and 'the (m.)', ka 'she' and 'the (f.)'. A noun subject is echoed by its marker: u Bah u wan (Bah, he comes).

items.target: ïa nga, ïa me/pha/phi, ïa u, ïa ka, ïa i, ïa ngi, ïa ki
items.gloss: me, you, him, her, it, us, them

example.target: U la ïohi ïa nga, hynrei ngam shym la ïohi ïa u.
example.gloss: He saw me, but I didn't see him.

items.note: Object pronouns are the subject pronouns with ïa in front; nothing else changes. ïa is also used before human and definite noun objects: nga ïohi ïa ka kmie.

items.target: not applicable: u / ka / i / ki mark gender and number, both 'a' and 'the'
items.gloss: no a/the distinction; the gender marker stands in for both

example.target: Nga don ka kali. Ka kali ka long ka thymmai.
example.gloss: I have a car. The car is new.

items.note: One marker does the job of a, the and the pronoun. 'A certain one' can be stressed with kawei/uwei after the noun: ka briew kawei (a certain woman).

items.target: u (masc.), ka (fem.), i (small, dear, neutral), ki (plural)
items.gloss: the four markers that every noun and pronoun carries

example.target: u ksew (dog), ka miaw (cat), i khun (little child), ki khun (children); ka ïing kaba heh
example.gloss: a dog, a cat, a small child, children; a house that is big

items.note: Learn every noun with its marker: sun is u sngi, moon is u bnai, most abstracts and big things are ka. Adjectives take the marker again with ba: ka ïing kaba heh.

items.target: ki + noun (ka ïing → ki ïing); people counted with ngut, things with tylli
items.gloss: plural: swap the marker to ki; the noun never changes

example.target: Ka khun kawei, ki khun lai ngut; ka kot kawei, ki kot ar tylli.
example.gloss: One child, three children; one book, two books.

items.note: The noun has no plural ending; ki carries the whole plural. A number goes with a classifier: ar ngut ki briew (two people), lai tylli ki ïing (three houses).

items.target: kane/une/ine/kine (this, these) / kata/uta/ita/kita (that, those) / katai/utai (that over there)
items.gloss: this / that / these / those, by gender and distance

example.target: Kane ka kot ka long jong nga; kata ka jong u.
example.gloss: This book is mine; that one is his.

items.note: The demonstrative is the marker plus -ne (near), -ta (there, or already mentioned), -tai (visible, far), -tei (up), -thie (down). It follows the noun's gender.

items.target: wei, ar, lai, saw, san, hynriew, hynñiew, phra, khyndai, shiphew, khadwei ... arphew, laiphew ... shispah

example.target: khadar (12), arphew san (25), sanphew (50), shispah (100); ba nyngkong, ba ar (1st, 2nd)
example.gloss: 12, 25, 50, 100; first, second

items.note: 11-19 are khad plus the digit (khadwei, khadar, khadlai), tens are digit plus phew (arphew, laiphew). Ordinals: ba nyngkong (first), then ba + number: ka sngi ba ar (the second day).

items.target: ka kyrteng (name), u/ka Khasi (a Khasi), u/ka nongtrei (worker), u/ka nonghikai (teacher), u/ka nongpule (student), u/ka doktor (doctor), u/ka nongrep (farmer), u/ka nongdie (shopkeeper), ka kam (job), ka rta (age), u snem (year), ka ri (country), ka shnong (village, home town), ka ktien (language), u/ka lok (friend)
items.gloss: Self: name, nationality, job, age
items.note: Job nouns take nong- plus the verb (trei, hikai, pule, rep, die) and the marker shows the person's sex. Age: nga don arphew snem (I have twenty years).

items.target: u kpa (father), ka kmie (mother), u bah (elder brother), ka kong (elder sister), u/ka para (brother, sister), u khun (son), ka khun (daughter), ki khun (children), u kñi (maternal uncle), ka meikha (father's mother), ka ïawbei (grandmother, ancestress), u tnga (husband), ka tnga (wife), u briew (man, person), ka kynthei (woman), ka kur (clan)
items.gloss: Family and people
items.note: Khasi is matrilineal: ka kur (the clan) and ka ïawbei pass through the mother, and u kñi (mother's brother) matters more than in English families. Bah and Kong are also polite address to any older man or woman.

items.target: ka ja (cooked rice), ka jingbam (food), ka doh (meat), u dohkha (fish), ka doh syiar (chicken), ka doh sniang (pork), ka jhur (vegetables), u soh (fruit), ka um (water), ka sha (tea), ka kophi (coffee), ka dud (milk), ka jadoh (rice cooked with meat), ka tungrymbai (fermented soybean), ka kwai (betel nut), ka bil (bill)
items.gloss: Food and drink, ordering
items.note: bam is eat, dih is drink, bam kwai (chew betel) is how you are welcomed. ja is cooked rice and stands for 'a meal': phi lah bam ja? means 'have you eaten?'.

items.target: ka por (time), ka sngi (day), ka miet (night), mynstep (morning), mynsngi (midday), janmiet (evening), mynta (now), mynta ka sngi (today), mynhynnin (yesterday), lashai (tomorrow), ka taiew (week), u bnai (month), u snem (year), baje (o'clock), ka minit (minute), man ka sngi (every day)
items.gloss: Time, days, months, clock
items.note: Days and months use the English names after the Khasi marker: ka sngi Sunday, u bnai January. Clock: san baje (five o'clock), san baje bad ar shiphew minit (five twenty).

items.target: ka shnong (village, town), ka ïew (market), ka dukan (shop), ka ïing (house), ka ïing bam (restaurant), ka skul (school), ka balang (church), ka ospital (hospital), ka bas stand (bus stand), ka lynti (road), ka jaka (place), hangne (here), hangta (there), beit (straight), sha kti mon (to the right), sha kti diang (to the left), jan (near), jngai (far)
items.gloss: Places in town, directions
items.note: Iewduh (Bara Bazar) is the market; leit sha ïew is 'go shopping'. Directions come as bare imperatives: leit beit, kylla sha kti mon (go straight, turn right).

items.target: leit (go), wan (come), bam (eat), dih (drink), ïohi (see), leh (do), shna (make), ong (say), tip (know), ai (give), shim (take), shong (live, sit), trei (work), thied (buy), kren (speak), pule (read, study), thoh (write), thiah (sleep), lehkai (play), nang (learn), kwah (want), ieid (like, love), donkam (need), don (have), long/dei (be)
items.gloss: The 25 core verbs
items.note: Every verb is one unchanging root; the particles la, yn, dang, lah, ym do all the work. pule is both read and study, shong is both sit and live somewhere.

items.target: ñ (palatal nasal); ï (y-glide); aspirated kh/th/ph vs plain k/t/p; y as schwa; word-initial ng
items.gloss: ñ is the ny of 'canyon' (khlaiñ, kñi). ï is a consonant y, so ïa is 'ya' and ïing is 'ying'. kh, th, ph have an audible puff of air and contrast with k, t, p: ka (the, she) and kha (to give birth) are different words. y between consonants is a short unstressed uh (kynthei is kuhn-THEI, pyrthei puhr-THEI). nga, ngi, ngut begin with the ng of 'sing'; do not add a vowel before it.

items.target: stress on the last syllable of the root; prefixes jing-, pyn-, nong- unstressed; Latin script with ñ and ï
items.gloss: Stress the final syllable: bam, jingBAM, nongTREI, pynKHREH. English speakers front-stress long words and become hard to follow. Script is the Latin alphabet with ñ and ï as extra letters; older books write ia for ïa. Final p, t, k are stopped without release (dep, bait, dak), and there is no z, v or f except in loanwords.

items.target: Khublei / Kumno? / Leit suk (go well) / Shong suk (stay well)
items.gloss: Hello, thanks, goodbye / How are you? / Go well / Stay well

example.target: Khublei, Bah! — Khublei. Kumno? — Bha hi. Ngan leit noh, shong suk. — Leit suk.
example.gloss: Hello, Bah! — Hello. How are you? — Fine. I'm off, stay well. — Go well.

items.note: Khublei (God bless) is the universal greeting and thank-you. Goodbyes are a pair: the one leaving says shong suk, the one staying says leit suk; swap them and it sounds odd.

items.target: sngewbha / Khublei shibun / Khublei, ym don eiei
items.gloss: please / thank you very much / you're welcome

example.target: Ai ïa nga ka um, sngewbha. — Kane. — Khublei shibun. — Khublei.
example.gloss: Give me water, please. — Here. — Thanks a lot. — You're welcome.

items.note: sngewbha (literally 'feel good') is placed at the end or start of a request. shibun (very, a lot) strengthens Khublei. Thanks is answered with Khublei back.

items.target: Map ïa nga / Map (excuse me) / Nga sngewsih
items.gloss: Forgive me / Excuse me / I'm sorry (I feel sad)

example.target: Map, Kong, hangno ka ospital? — Map ïa nga, ngam tip.
example.gloss: Excuse me, Kong, where is the hospital? — Sorry, I don't know.

items.note: map is 'forgive'. A bare Map opens a request to a stranger; Map ïa nga apologises for a fault. Nga sngewsih expresses sympathy or regret, not an apology.

items.target: Katno kane? / Katno ka dor?
items.gloss: How much is this? / How much is the price?

example.target: Katno kane ka bag? — Sanspah tyngka. — Kham rit khyndiat, sngewbha.
example.gloss: How much is this bag? — Five hundred rupees. — A little less, please.

items.note: katno is 'how much, how many'. Bargaining is expected at Iewduh: kham rit khyndiat (a little smaller) is the polite counter-offer.

items.target: Hangno ka ___? / Hangno u ___?
items.gloss: Where is the ___?

example.target: Hangno ka ïing pule? — Hangta, jan ka balang.
example.gloss: Where is the library? — There, near the church.

items.note: The marker of the noun must follow hangno: hangno ka skul, hangno u Bah. hangta (there) or ha kata ka lynti (on that road) is the usual answer.

items.target: Ngam sngewthuh / Ngam sngewthuh bha
items.gloss: I don't understand / I don't understand well

example.target: Map, ngam sngewthuh. Phi lah ban kren ka ktien English?
example.gloss: Sorry, I don't understand. Can you speak English?

items.note: ngam is nga plus ym fused; say it as one word. sngewthuh is understand by hearing; tip is know. Add bha (well) to soften: ngam sngewthuh bha.

items.target: Sngewbha ong biang / Sngewbha kren kham suki
items.gloss: Please say it again / Please speak more slowly

example.target: Sngewbha ong biang, kham suki khyndiat.
example.gloss: Please say it again, a little more slowly.

items.note: biang is 'again'; kham suki is 'more slowly'. sngewbha at the front makes the bare imperative polite; ong (say) is used for repeating words.

items.target: Ka kyrteng jong nga ka long ___ / Nga sngewkmen ban ïakynduh ïa phi
items.gloss: My name is ___ / I'm glad to meet you

example.target: Ka kyrteng jong nga ka long Arjun. Nga sngewkmen ban ïakynduh ïa phi.
example.gloss: My name is Arjun. I'm glad to meet you.

items.note: kyrteng (name) is feminine, so it is ka kyrteng and the verb is echoed by ka: ka kyrteng jong nga ka long. Asking: Kumno ka kyrteng jong phi?

items.target: Phi kwah ban ___ bad nga? / Wan ___ lem bad ngi
items.gloss: Do you want to ___ with me? / Come ___ with us

example.target: Phi kwah ban leit bam janmiet ha ka sngi Friday bad nga?
example.gloss: Do you want to go out for dinner on Friday with me?

items.note: Uses C-WOULD-YOU-LIKE and D-LETS. The invitation is a plain yes/no question; the softener is the tone and phi, not a conditional verb.

items.target: Bha, ngan wan! / Khublei, hynrei ngam lah, namar ba ___
items.gloss: Good, I'll come! / Thanks, but I can't, because ___

example.target: Khublei, hynrei ngam lah ban wan namar ba nga hap ban trei haduh lait.
example.gloss: Thanks, but I can't come because I have to work until late.

items.note: Uses C-THANKS-BUT, D-CAN, G-BECAUSE, D-HAVE-TO. Refusals always carry a namar ba reason; a bare em (no) is abrupt.

items.target: Kumno lada ___? / To ngi ___
items.gloss: How about ___? / Let's ___

example.target: Kumno lada ngin ïakynduh ha ka sngi Saturday, ha ïew? — Bha, kumta.
example.gloss: How about we meet on Saturday, at the market? — Good, like that.

items.note: Uses C-HOW-ABOUT, D-LETS, G-AT. Kumno lada (how if) opens a suggestion; the reply Bha, kumta (good, so) or Bha hi accepts it.

items.target: Map ïa nga, ___ / Nga sngewsih shibun ba ___
items.gloss: Forgive me, ___ / I'm very sorry that ___

example.target: Map ïa nga ba nga la wan lait, ka bas ka la sah ha lynti.
example.gloss: Sorry I came late, the bus was stuck on the road.

items.note: Uses C-SORRY, C-SORRY-LATE, G-BECAUSE. Map ïa nga plus ba (that) and the explanation; the reply is Ym don eiei (it's nothing).

items.target: Ai ïa nga ___, sngewbha / Aiu kane? / Ka bil, sngewbha
items.gloss: Give me ___, please / What is this? / The bill, please

example.target: Ai ïa nga ka jadoh kawei bad ka sha, sngewbha. Hadien kata ka bil, sngewbha.
example.gloss: One jadoh and a tea, please. After that the bill, please.

items.note: Uses D-WOULD-LIKE, C-BILL, C-WHAT-MEAN. Ordering is the imperative ai plus sngewbha; kawei after the dish counts one portion.

items.target: Kaei ka jingmut jong ___? / Kumno ban ong ___ ha ka Khasi?
items.gloss: What is the meaning of ___? / How do you say ___ in Khasi?

example.target: Kaei ka jingmut jong 'khlaiñ'? — Ka mut 'strong', 'healthy'.
example.gloss: What does 'khlaiñ' mean? — It means strong, healthy.

items.note: Uses C-WHAT-MEAN, C-REPEAT-PLEASE. jingmut is the noun 'meaning', mut the verb 'to mean'; kaei (which, f.) asks after a feminine noun.

items.target: Nyngkong nga la ___, hadien kata nga la ___
items.gloss: First I ___, after that I ___

example.target: Nyngkong nga la leit sha balang, hadien kata nga la bam bad ka ïing jong nga.
example.gloss: First I went to church, after that I ate with my family.

items.note: Uses T-PAST, G-SEQUENCE, G-BEFORE-AFTER. la on the first verb sets the past; later verbs may drop it once the time is clear.

items.target: Lano bad hangno ngin ïakynduh? / Bha, ha ___ baje ha ___
items.gloss: When and where shall we meet? / Fine, at ___ o'clock at ___

example.target: Lano ngin ïakynduh? — Ha saw baje, ha Police Bazar. — Bha, sa ïakynduh.
example.gloss: When shall we meet? — At four, at Police Bazar. — Fine, see you then.

items.note: Uses D-LETS, G-AT, C-SEE-YOU, C-SOUNDS-GOOD. ïakynduh (meet each other) carries the reciprocal prefix ïa-; no object is needed.

items.target: nga hap ban ___
items.gloss: I have to ___

example.target: Nga hap ban trei haduh lait mynta ka sngi.
example.gloss: I have to work late today.

items.note: hap is external obligation (something falls on you); dei is duty or advice. Both take ban before the verb. Negative: ngam hap ban (I don't have to).

items.target: nga dei ban ___ / phim dei ban ___
items.gloss: I must ___ / you must not ___

example.target: Phi dei ban wan ha por. Phim dei ban leit ïaid ha ka miet.
example.gloss: You must come on time. You must not go walking at night.

items.note: phim dei ban is a prohibition (mustn't), not 'need not'; for 'no need' say phim donkam ban. The blunt prohibition is wat plus verb: Wat leit!

items.target: phi dei ban ___ / kham bha lada phi ___
items.gloss: you should ___ / it would be better if you ___

example.target: Phi dei ban shongthiah kham bun; kham bha lada phi dih ka um shibun.
example.gloss: You should rest more; it'd be better if you drank a lot of water.

items.note: dei ban is must and should at once; kham bha lada (better if) is the softer advice form. Context and tone decide how strong dei sounds.

items.target: phi lah ban ___? / nga la lah ban ___
items.gloss: could you ___? / I could ___ (was able to)

example.target: Phi lah ban ïarap ïa nga khyndiat? Mynshwa nga la lah ban ïaid jngai.
example.gloss: Could you help me a little? Before, I could walk far.

items.note: The request is just D-CAN as a question with sngewbha; past ability adds la before lah: nga la lah ban. Khasi has no separate 'could'.

items.target: lehse ___ / ka lah ban ___
items.gloss: maybe ___ / it can (might) ___

example.target: Lehse kan slap janmiet, shim ka syrbaïn.
example.gloss: It might rain this evening, take the umbrella.

items.note: lehse (perhaps) is an adverb at the front and is the normal way to say might; it needs no special verb form. lah ban long (can be) is the heavier option.

items.target: mynshwa nga ju ___ / nga la ju ___
items.gloss: before, I used to ___ / I habitually ___ (past)

example.target: Mynshwa nga ju leit sha ïew man ka sngi bad ka kmie jong nga.
example.gloss: I used to go to the market every day with my mother.

items.note: ju marks habit; mynshwa (formerly) or la puts it in the past. Negative habit: ngam ju (I never do). la ju also gives 'have ever done'.

items.target: nga la ju ___ / ngam pat ___
items.gloss: I have (ever) ___ / I haven't ___ yet

example.target: Phi la ju leit sha Sohra? — Em, ngam pat leit.
example.gloss: Have you ever been to Sohra? — No, I haven't been yet.

items.note: Experience is la ju (have ever), 'not yet' is ym pat, 'already' is lah (nga lah bam). English present perfect splits three ways in Khasi.

items.target: nga dang ___ haba ___ / nga la dang ___
items.gloss: I was ___-ing when ___

example.target: Nga dang sum haba u phone u la ring.
example.gloss: I was bathing when the phone rang.

items.note: dang gives the background action, haba (when) brings in the event. la on dang is optional once the story is in the past.

items.target: nga kyrmen ban ___ / nga la thmu ban ___ / nga pyrshang ban ___
items.gloss: I hope to ___ / I have planned to ___ / I try to ___

example.target: Nga kyrmen ban wan biang sha Shillong u snem ba wan.
example.gloss: I hope to come back to Shillong next year.

items.note: Every verb-plus-verb link is ban: kyrmen ban (hope to), thmu ban (plan to), pyrshang ban (try to), klet ban (forget to), kular ban (promise to).

items.target: nga sngewtynnad ban ___ / nga dep ban ___ / nga dang ___ shuh
items.gloss: I enjoy ___-ing / I finish ___-ing / I keep on ___-ing

example.target: Nga sngewtynnad ban pule ki kot Khasi ha ka miet.
example.gloss: I enjoy reading Khasi books at night.

items.note: Khasi has no -ing form: the second verb takes ban whether English uses to or -ing. 'Keep doing' is dang plus verb plus shuh or the repeated verb.

items.target: nga pyrkhat ba ___ / nga tip ba ___
items.gloss: I think that ___ / I know that ___

example.target: Nga pyrkhat ba kan slap lashai, hynrei ngam tip shisha.
example.gloss: I think it will rain tomorrow, but I don't know for sure.

items.note: ba is the clause link after pyrkhat, tip, ong, ngeit, sngew. It is never dropped, unlike English 'that'. Word order after ba is unchanged.

items.target: to ngi ___ / ngin ___, hooid?
items.gloss: let's ___ / we'll ___, yes?

example.target: To ngi leit bam ja hangta. — Hooid, to ngi leit.
example.gloss: Let's go eat there. — Yes, let's go.

items.note: to is the softening imperative particle; to ngi plus verb is 'let us'. 'Shall we?' is the future ngin plus rising tone or ne em.

items.target: pronoun + (la) dang + verb
items.gloss: past continuous: dang, with la optional

example.target: Ki la dang bam haba nga la poi.
example.gloss: They were eating when I arrived.

items.note: The same dang as the present progressive; only la (or the context) makes it past. Khasi has no imperfect: habit in the past is ju, not dang.

items.target: pronoun + lah + verb (already) / la ju + verb (ever) / ym pat + verb (not yet)
items.gloss: present perfect: three particles for three meanings

example.target: Nga lah trei dep. Phi la ju bam ka jadoh? Ngam pat bam.
example.gloss: I have finished working. Have you ever eaten jadoh? I haven't yet.

items.note: There is no single present perfect. Result: lah; experience: la ju; unfinished: ym pat. dep after the verb means 'finished'.

items.target: Lada ___ (present), ___ yn ___

example.target: Lada ka slap lashai, ngan sah ha ïing.
example.gloss: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay at home.

items.note: lada plus the bare verb, then the future yn in the main clause. No 'will' is allowed inside the lada clause, same as English.

items.target: time word + present / ngan ___ + time word
items.gloss: present or plain future with a time word for arranged plans

example.target: Lashai nga ïakynduh bad ka lok jong nga ha Laitumkhrah.
example.gloss: Tomorrow I'm meeting my friend at Laitumkhrah.

items.note: Arranged plans use the bare verb plus lashai, ha ka sngi Sunday, etc. Adding yn is also fine; dang would wrongly mean 'in the middle of'.

items.target: verb (Wan!) / To + verb (To wan) / Wat + verb (don't) / verb + sngewbha
items.gloss: imperative: bare verb, softened by To or sngewbha, negated by Wat

example.target: Shong! To shong hangne, sngewbha. Wat leit noh!
example.gloss: Sit! Please sit here. Don't go away!

items.note: The bare verb is the imperative to friends and children; To in front or sngewbha after makes it polite. Wat is the only negative imperative.

items.target: ___, kumta ___ / namarkata ___
items.gloss: ___, so ___ / therefore ___

example.target: Ka bas ka la sah, kumta nga la wan lait.
example.gloss: The bus was stuck, so I came late.

items.note: kumta (like that, so) opens the result clause; namarkata (because of that) is heavier. Don't confuse with kumta as a reply meaning 'OK, fine'.

items.target: haba ___ / mynba ___ (past time)
items.gloss: when ___ / when (back when) ___

example.target: Haba phi poi, phone ïa nga. Mynba nga dang khynnah, nga la shong ha Sohra.
example.gloss: When you arrive, phone me. When I was a child, I lived in Sohra.

items.note: haba is the general 'when'; mynba is only for a past period. Neither changes word order. The question 'when?' is lano, not haba.

items.target: shwa ba ___ / hadien ba ___ / ynda ___
items.gloss: before ___ / after ___ / once, after ___

example.target: Sait ka kti shwa ba phi bam; hadien ba phi bam, sait ki plet.
example.gloss: Wash your hands before you eat; after you eat, wash the plates.

items.note: shwa and hadien take ba before a clause and jong or a noun directly (shwa ka por bam). ynda is 'once X has happened', common in instructions.

items.target: lada ___
items.gloss: if ___

example.target: Lada phi don ka por, wan sha ïing jong nga.
example.gloss: If you have time, come to my house.

items.note: lada starts the condition and nothing else moves. lada ym is 'if not, unless'; lada tang is 'if only'. 'Whether' in reported questions is also lada.

items.gloss: ___ that ___ (clause link)

example.target: Nga tip ba phi dang trei, hynrei nga donkam ban kren bad phi.
example.gloss: I know that you're working, but I need to talk with you.

items.note: ba is compulsory after saying, thinking and knowing verbs. The same ba builds relative clauses with a marker in front (uba, kaba, kiba).

items.target: u ___ uba ___ / ka ___ kaba ___ / ki ___ kiba ___
items.gloss: the (m.) ___ who ___ / the (f.) ___ which ___ / the (pl.) ___ that ___

example.target: U briew uba dang kren ha khmat u dei u nonghikai jong nga.
example.gloss: The man who is speaking at the front is my teacher.

items.note: The relative word is the noun's marker plus ba: uba, kaba, iba, kiba. Get the marker wrong and the sentence points at a different noun.

items.target: ___ naduh ___ (since) / ___ ar snem (for two years)
items.gloss: since ___ / for ___ (a length of time)

example.target: Nga shong ha Shillong naduh 2020, kata ka long ar snem.
example.gloss: I've lived in Shillong since 2020, that is two years.

items.note: naduh marks the starting point; a length of time is just the number plus unit (lai snem, shi taiew) with no preposition. The verb stays present.

items.target: haduh ___ / haduh ba ___
items.gloss: until ___ / until (the time that) ___

example.target: Ap hangne haduh ba nga wan biang.
example.gloss: Wait here until I come back.

items.note: haduh is 'up to' for both place and time (haduh Sohra, haduh lait). Before a clause add ba. 'By (a deadline)' is also haduh.

items.target: shaphang ___
items.gloss: about, concerning ___

example.target: Ngi la ïakren shaphang ka kam bad ka jingpule.
example.gloss: We talked about work and studies.

items.note: shaphang introduces a topic after kren, ïakren, tip, pyrkhat. 'About' meaning roughly is a different word: kumba (about five) or ban ïa.

items.target: nyngkong, ___ / hadien kata, ___ / hadien, ___ / ha kaba kut, ___
items.gloss: first, ___ / after that, ___ / later, ___ / finally, ___

example.target: Nyngkong ngi la leit sha Sohra, hadien kata sha Mawsmai, ha kaba kut ngi la wan biang.
example.gloss: First we went to Sohra, after that to Mawsmai, finally we came back.

items.note: nyngkong (first), hadien kata (after that), ha kaba kut (at the end) sit at the front of each step. la is set once and may be dropped later.

items.target: jong nga, jong me/pha/phi, jong u, jong ka, jong i, jong ngi, jong ki (after the noun)
items.gloss: my, your, his, her, its, our, their

example.target: Ka ïing jong nga ka don jan ka ïing jong ki.
example.gloss: My house is near their house.

items.note: Possession is noun plus jong plus pronoun; the noun keeps its own marker (ka ïing jong u, his house, even though u is male). Speech often drops jong: ka ïing nga.

items.target: bun (many, much), khyndiat (a little, few), shibun (a lot), katto katne (some), kiwei (some, others), kano kano / uno uno (any)
items.gloss: some, any, much, many, a lot of, a little

example.target: Don bun ki briew ha ïew; nga don khyndiat ka pisa; ai ïa nga katto katne ki soh.
example.gloss: There are many people at the market; I have a little money; give me some fruit.

items.note: Quantifiers come before the marked noun: bun ki briew, khyndiat ka pisa. No count/mass split: bun is many and much, khyndiat is few and little.

items.target: kham + adjective + ïa ___ (also: ban ïa ___)
items.gloss: more ___ than ___

example.target: Ka Sohra ka kham khriat ïa ka Shillong.
example.gloss: Sohra is colder than Shillong.

items.note: kham before the adjective is 'more', ïa (or ban ïa) introduces the standard. Subject nouns are echoed by the marker: ka Sohra ka kham khriat.

items.target: ___ eh (too) / ___ biang (enough) / ___ shibun (very) / ___ bha (well, quite)
items.gloss: too / enough / very

example.target: Kane ka dor ka jrong eh. Ka bha shibun, hynrei ngam don biang ka pisa.
example.gloss: This price is too high. It's very good, but I don't have enough money.

items.note: All four follow the adjective or verb they modify: heh eh (too big), bun biang (enough), bha shibun (very good). Before a noun biang goes first: biang ka pisa.

items.target: ïa ___ (to/for a person) / na ka bynta ___ (for the sake of)
items.gloss: indirect object: ïa, the same marker as the direct object

example.target: Ai ïa nga ka kot; nga la thied kane na ka bynta jong phi.
example.gloss: Give me the book; I bought this for you.

items.note: There is no dative: the recipient takes ïa just like a direct object, and comes first (ai ïa nga ka kot). na ka bynta jong is 'for the sake of, on behalf of'.

items.target: ka bas (bus), ka kali (car, vehicle), ka taxi (shared taxi), ka rel (train), ka tiket (ticket), ka lynti (road), ka jingleit (journey), u/ka nongpyniaid kali (driver), ka hotel (hotel), ka kamra (room), ka jaka shong (seat), ka bag (bag), ka kot (document, paper), poi (arrive), mih (leave, go out), ka bas stand (bus stand)
items.gloss: Travel, transport, tickets, hotel
items.note: Shillong's shared Maruti taxis are just ka taxi; you ask Shano phi leit? (where to?) and pay per seat. poi is arrive, mih is set out or go out.

items.target: ka dukan (shop), ka ïew (market), ka dor (price), ka pisa (money), ka tyngka (rupee), thied (buy), die (sell), ka jaiñ (cloth), ka jainsem (Khasi women's dress), ka sopti (shirt), ka juti (shoes), ka bag (bag), dor jrong (expensive), kham rit ka dor (cheaper), ka jingthied (purchase), katno (how much)
items.gloss: Shopping, clothes, money
items.note: Prices are ka dor, and dor jrong (high price) is expensive; ask kham rit khyndiat? (a bit less?) to bargain. dukan is any shop, ïew the open market.

items.target: ka met (body), ka khlieh (head), ka kti (hand, arm), ka kjat (foot, leg), ka khmat (eye), ka shkor (ear), ka kpoh (stomach), pang (be ill), ka jingpang (illness), sih (hurt, painful), ka dawai (medicine), u/ka doktor (doctor), ka ospital (hospital), khlaiñ (healthy, strong), ka jingkhlaiñ (health), ka jingsngew (feeling)
items.gloss: Health, body, at the doctor
items.note: Pain is the body part as subject plus sih: ka khlieh ka sih (my head hurts). pang is the verb 'be ill': nga dang pang (I'm ill right now).

items.target: ka kam (work, job), trei (work), ka ophis (office), u/ka nongtrei (worker), u/ka bah (boss, senior), ka meeting (meeting), ka skul (school), ka kolej (college), pule (study), u/ka nongpule (student), u/ka nonghikai (teacher), hikai (teach), ka jinghikai (lesson), ka jingkylli (question), ka jingjubab (answer), ka por trei (working hours)
items.gloss: Work and study
items.note: trei is the verb, ka kam the noun: nga trei ka kam ha ophis. Office loans stay English: meeting, email, deadline. hikai is teach, pule is study.

items.target: ka slap (rain), slap (to rain), u sngi (sun), ka lyer (wind), u lyoh (cloud), ka bneng (sky), shit (hot), ka jingshit (heat), khriat (cold), ka jingkhriat (cold), ka eriong (storm), ka por slap (rainy season), ka por khriat (winter), ka por shit (hot season), ka jingsngewbha (pleasant weather), ka syrbaïn (umbrella)
items.gloss: Weather and seasons
items.note: Weather sentences take ka as a dummy subject: ka slap (it rains), ka khriat (it's cold). Sohra's rain is the local small talk: ka slap shibun mynta.

items.target: ïeng (get up), sum (bathe), bam (eat), shet ja (cook rice), sait (wash), khreh (tidy, prepare), thiah (sleep), leit kam (go to work), wan sha ïing (come home), ka ïing (house), ka kamra (room), ka jingkhang (door), ka rympei (hearth, kitchen), ka ding (fire, stove), ka jingthiah (bed), sait jaiñ (do the laundry)
items.gloss: Daily routine, house, chores
items.note: A routine is told with man ka sngi plus bare verbs: man ka sngi nga ïeng ha hynriew baje. The rympei (hearth) is the centre of a traditional Khasi home.

items.target: content words stressed on the last syllable; markers u/ka/ki, la, yn, ban, ïa, jong unstressed
items.gloss: The little grammar words are nearly swallowed: u Bah u la leit sounds like uBAHu-la-LEIT. Each noun and verb keeps a firm final-syllable beat, so Khasi has a bouncing rhythm of weak-weak-STRONG groups. English speakers stress la or ïa and sound as if they are spelling the sentence out.

items.target: yes/no: rise on the last word, or the tag ne em with a fall; wh-questions fall
items.gloss: A yes/no question is the statement with a rise at the very end: Phi lah bam? Adding ne em makes the pitch fall on em and sounds relaxed, not challenging. Questions with aiu, mano, hangno fall like statements; the question word carries the emphasis.

items.target: Phi kwah ban ___? / Phi mon ban ___?
items.gloss: Do you want to ___? / Would you like to ___?

example.target: Phi kwah ban dih ka sha? — Hooid, khublei.
example.gloss: Would you like to drink tea? — Yes, thanks.

items.note: kwah is want; mon is the softer 'wish, be willing', so Phi mon ban is the politer offer. Accepting is hooid plus khublei, declining em plus khublei.

items.target: Khublei, hynrei ___ / Ka bha shibun, hynrei ___
items.gloss: Thanks, but ___ / That's very kind, but ___

example.target: Khublei, hynrei ngam lah ban wan mynta ka sngi.
example.gloss: Thanks, but I can't come today.

items.note: hynrei straight after the thanks is the polite refusal frame; follow it with namar ba and a reason to keep it warm.

items.target: Kumno lada ___? / Bad ___ te?
items.gloss: How about ___? / And ___ then?

example.target: Kumno lada ngin leit ha ka sngi Sunday? — Bad ka sngi Saturday te?
example.gloss: How about we go on Sunday? — And Saturday then?

items.note: Kumno lada (how if) takes a full clause; Bad ... te? takes a noun and is the quick counter-proposal. Both end in a rise.

items.target: Map ïa nga ba nga la wan lait
items.gloss: Sorry that I came late

example.target: Map ïa nga ba nga la wan lait, ka lynti ka la jam shibun.
example.gloss: Sorry I'm late, the road was very jammed.

items.note: lait is late; the apology uses the past la wan lait because the arriving is done. Reply: Ym don eiei, wan shong (no problem, come sit).

items.target: Ka bil, sngewbha / Katno baroh?
items.gloss: The bill, please / How much altogether?

example.target: Bah, ka bil, sngewbha. Katno baroh? — Sanspah tyngka.
example.gloss: Bah, the bill, please. How much altogether? — Five hundred rupees.

items.note: bil is the English loan and universal. baroh is 'all, altogether'. Address the waiter as Bah or Kong, never with me or pha.

items.target: Kaei ka jingmut jong ___? / ___ ka mut aiu?
items.gloss: What is the meaning of ___? / ___ means what?

example.target: Kaei ka jingmut jong 'dohneiiong'? — Ka mut ka doh sniang ba ïong.
example.gloss: What does 'dohneiiong' mean? — It means pork that is black.

items.note: jingmut (meaning) is ka, so the question word is kaei (which one, f.). The answer starts ka mut (it means).

items.target: Sa ïakynduh / Sa ïakynduh lashai / Sa ïohi biang
items.gloss: See you / See you tomorrow / See you again

example.target: Bha, sa ïakynduh lashai ha saw baje. Leit suk!
example.gloss: Right, see you tomorrow at four. Go well!

items.note: sa (later) plus the verb, with no pronoun, is the standard sign-off. Add the time word straight after the verb.

items.target: Bha, kumta / Bha hi / Biang
items.gloss: Good, like that / Fine / OK, that'll do

example.target: Ngin ïakynduh ha Police Bazar? — Bha, kumta.
example.gloss: We'll meet at Police Bazar? — Sounds good.

items.note: bha is good, kumta is 'like that', so Bha, kumta accepts a plan. Biang (enough) is the casual 'OK' and also stops a waiter pouring.

items.target: Ha ka jingpeit jong nga, ___ / Phi pyrkhat kumno?
items.gloss: In my view, ___ / What do you think?

example.target: Ha ka jingpeit jong nga, ka jingtrei na ïing ka bha. Phi pyrkhat kumno?
example.gloss: In my view, working from home is good. What do you think?

items.note: Uses C-IN-MY-OPINION, D-THINK-THAT, C-WHAT-DO-YOU-THINK. jingpeit (view) and jingmut (opinion) are interchangeable here.

items.target: Nga mynjur / Ngam mynjur / Nga mynjur khyndiat, hynrei ___
items.gloss: I agree / I don't agree / I partly agree, but ___

example.target: Nga mynjur bad phi ha kata, hynrei ngam mynjur ba ka kam ka kham khlaiñ.
example.gloss: I agree with you on that, but I don't agree that the work is harder.

items.note: Uses C-I-AGREE, C-SEE-POINT-BUT, G-BUT. mynjur bad (agree with a person), mynjur ba (agree that). Khasi softens disagreement with hynrei, not with 'well'.

items.target: namar ba ___ / kum u nuksa, ___ / ka daw ba nyngkong ka long ___
items.gloss: because ___ / for example, ___ / the first reason is ___

example.target: Ka daw ba nyngkong: ka dor ka jrong. Kum u nuksa, ka kamra ka long shispah tyngka.
example.gloss: The first reason: the price is high. For example, a room is a hundred rupees.

items.note: Uses G-BECAUSE, G-SO, C-THE-THING-IS. daw is reason; nuksa is example and takes the marker u. Reasons are numbered with ba nyngkong, ba ar.

items.target: Mynba ___, nga dang ___ / Ynda ___, ___ / hadien kata ___
items.gloss: Back when ___, I was ___-ing / Once ___, ___ / after that ___

example.target: Mynba nga dang leit sha skul, ka slap ka la sdang; hadien kata nga la ïeng ha ka dukan.
example.gloss: When I was going to school, the rain started; after that I stood in a shop.

items.note: Uses D-WAS-DOING, G-WHEN, G-SEQUENCE, D-HAD-DONE. Background takes dang, events take la; la lah marks the earlier of two past events.

items.target: Map, hynrei don ka jingeh: ___ / Phi lah ban ___, sngewbha?
items.gloss: Excuse me, but there's a problem: ___ / Could you ___, please?

example.target: Map, Bah, don ka jingeh: ka wifi kam trei. Phi lah ban kylla ka kamra ïa nga, sngewbha?
example.gloss: Excuse me, there's a problem: the wifi doesn't work. Could you change my room, please?

items.note: Uses C-THE-THING-IS, D-COULD, G-AND. jingeh is difficulty or problem. Complaints open with Map and stay in the polite phi form throughout.

items.target: Kumno lada ___? / Kata kam long, namar ba ___ / Te, ___ noh
items.gloss: How about ___? / That won't work, because ___ / Then, let's just ___

example.target: Kumno lada ha ka sngi Saturday? — Kam long, nga hap ban trei. — Te, Sunday noh.
example.gloss: How about Saturday? — That won't work, I have to work. — Then Sunday, then.

items.note: Uses C-HOW-ABOUT, G-BECAUSE, D-WOULD-RATHER, C-SOUNDS-GOOD. kam long (it won't do) rejects; noh after the compromise means 'just, then'.

items.target: Phi dei ban ___ / Lada nga long phi, ngan ___ / Wat ___!
items.gloss: You should ___ / If I were you, I'd ___ / Don't ___!

example.target: Phi dei ban leit sha doktor. Lada nga long phi, ngan shongthiah ha ïing. Wat leit trei!
example.gloss: You should go to the doctor. If I were you, I'd rest at home. Don't go to work!

items.note: Uses D-SHOULD, C-IF-I-WERE-YOU, T-IMPERATIVE. Warnings are the wat imperative plus a namar ba reason; no special modal is needed.

items.target: U la ong ba ___ / Ka la kylli lada ___ / Ka la ong ïa nga ban ___
items.gloss: He said that ___ / She asked whether ___ / She told me to ___

example.target: Ka bah ka la ong ba ka por kut ka long Thursday, bad ka la ong ïa nga ban ïathuh ïa ki.
example.gloss: The boss said the deadline is Thursday, and told me to tell them.

items.note: Uses D-SAID-THAT, D-TOLD-TO, G-THAT. Tenses do not shift after ong ba; only pronouns and time words change.

items.target: nga la lah ___ shwa ba ___
items.gloss: I had already ___ before ___

example.target: Nga la lah bam dep shwa ba u lok jong nga u la poi.
example.gloss: I had already finished eating before my friend arrived.

items.note: la lah (past plus already) is the pluperfect; shwa ba (before) or haba (when) supplies the later event. dep after the verb adds 'finished'.

items.target: nga dang ___ naduh ___ / nga la ___ ___ snem
items.gloss: I have been ___-ing since ___ / I have ___ for ___ years

example.target: Nga dang nang ka ktien Khasi naduh u snem ba la leit.
example.gloss: I have been learning Khasi since last year.

items.note: Present dang plus naduh (since) covers the English perfect progressive; the verb stays present because the action is ongoing. A duration needs no preposition.

items.target: u dei ban long ___ / um lah ban long ___
items.gloss: he must be ___ / he can't be ___

example.target: U dei ban long u nongtrei thymmai; um lah ban long u bah.
example.gloss: He must be the new worker; he can't be the boss.

items.note: Deduction borrows dei ban (must) and lah ban (can) with long (be). Speech often prefers the adverb: lehse u dei u nongtrei thymmai (probably he's ...).

items.target: nga la dei ban ___ / lada tang nga la ___
items.gloss: I should have ___ / if only I had ___

example.target: Nga la dei ban pule kham bun shwa ka exam.
example.gloss: I should have studied more before the exam.

items.note: la before dei ban gives 'should have, was supposed to'; the same form also means 'had to', so context decides. lada tang plus la is the regret version.

items.target: nga la lah ban ___ / lehse u la ___
items.gloss: I could have ___ / maybe he ___ (might have)

example.target: Nga la lah ban wan, hynrei nga la klet. Lehse u la leit noh.
example.gloss: I could have come, but I forgot. Maybe he has left.

items.note: la lah ban is past ability whether or not it was used. 'Might have' is not a verb form at all: lehse plus the plain past does the job.

items.target: nga kham kwah ban ___ / nga kham ieid ban ___
items.gloss: I'd rather ___ / I'd prefer to ___

example.target: Nga kham kwah ban leit sha ki lum ban ïa ka lyngkha bynta.
example.gloss: I'd rather go to the hills than to the seaside.

items.note: kham (more) before kwah or ieid makes the preference; the rejected option follows ban ïa (than). No conditional is needed.

items.target: lada nga long ___, ngan ___
items.gloss: if I were ___, I would ___

example.target: Lada nga long u riewspah, ngan thied ka ïing ha Sohra.
example.gloss: If I were rich, I would buy a house in Sohra.

items.note: Khasi's second conditional looks exactly like the first: lada plus bare verb, then yn. Unreality comes from the content, not from the verb.

items.target: nga kwah ba nga ___ / lada tang nga lah ban ___
items.gloss: I wish I ___ / if only I could ___

example.target: Lada tang nga lah ban kren ka Khasi kum u Khasi hi!
example.gloss: If only I could speak Khasi like a real Khasi!

items.note: There is no 'wish' verb form: kwah ba (want that) plus a clause, or lada tang (if only) left hanging. hi at the end adds 'genuinely, actually'.

items.target: ka la ong ïa nga ban ___ / ka la pan ïa nga ban ___
items.gloss: she told me to ___ / she asked me to ___

example.target: Ka kmie ka la ong ïa nga ban thied ka jhur na ïew.
example.gloss: Mother told me to buy vegetables from the market.

items.note: ong ïa (say to) plus ban is 'tell to'; pan ïa (request) is softer. kylli is only 'ask a question', never 'ask to do'.

items.target: u la ong ba ___ / u la kylli lada ___
items.gloss: he said that ___ / he asked whether ___

example.target: U la ong ba un wan lashai, bad u la kylli lada phi dang pang.
example.gloss: He said he'd come tomorrow, and asked whether you were still ill.

items.note: The reported clause keeps its original particles: un wan stays future, dang pang stays present. lada doubles as 'whether'.

items.target: phi lah ban ïathuh ïa nga hangno ___? / phi tip lada ___?
items.gloss: could you tell me where ___? / do you know whether ___?

example.target: Phi lah ban ïathuh ïa nga hangno ka bas sha Sohra ka mih?
example.gloss: Could you tell me where the bus to Sohra leaves from?

items.note: ïathuh is 'tell, inform'. The embedded question keeps its question word and normal order; nothing inverts. lada handles 'whether'.

items.target: ka la ___ ha ___ / ka la shna da ___ / ka shna na ___
items.gloss: it was ___ in ___ / it was made by ___ / it is made of ___

example.target: Kane ka balang ka la shna ha u snem 1890; ka shna na ka maw.
example.gloss: This church was built in 1890; it is made of stone.

items.note: There is no passive: the thing simply becomes the subject of la plus verb (ka la shna, it was built). The agent, if needed, takes da: da ki Welsh.

items.target: nga la nang ban ___ / nga dang nang ban ___
items.gloss: I'm used to ___-ing / I'm getting used to ___-ing

example.target: Nga la nang ban bam ka jingbam kaba shit; nga dang nang ban ïeng shwa.
example.gloss: I'm used to eating spicy food; I'm getting used to getting up early.

items.note: nang means both 'learn' and 'become accustomed', so la nang is 'be used to' and dang nang is 'getting used to'. It takes ban, or ïa before a noun.

items.target: ka la ai lad ïa nga ban ___ / ka la pynhap ïa nga ban ___
items.gloss: she let me ___ / she made me ___

example.target: Ka la ai lad ïa nga ban leit, hynrei ka la pynhap ïa nga ban wan biang shwa ka miet.
example.gloss: She let me go, but made me come back before night.

items.note: ai lad (give way) is 'allow'. 'Make someone' uses the causative prefix pyn- (pynhap, oblige; pynbam, feed). pyn- is productive: pynshong, pynïeng.

items.target: nga dei ban ___ / kham bha lada phi ___
items.gloss: I'm supposed to ___ / you'd better ___

example.target: Nga dei ban poi ha ophis ha khyndai baje; kham bha lada phi mih shwa.
example.gloss: I'm supposed to be in the office at nine; you'd better leave early.

items.note: dei ban covers should, must and supposed to. kham bha lada (better if) is the 'you'd better' warning, softened further with noh at the end.

items.target: ngan lah ban ___ / nga la lah ban ___
items.gloss: I'll be able to ___ / I was able to ___

example.target: U snem ba wan ngan lah ban kren ka Khasi; mynhynnin nga la lah ban sngewthuh baroh.
example.gloss: Next year I'll be able to speak Khasi; yesterday I could understand everything.

items.note: Because lah ban is a particle, not a verb, it takes yn and la like any verb: ngan lah ban, nga la lah ban. No substitute verb is needed.

items.target: pronoun + la lah + verb (+ dep)
items.gloss: past perfect: la plus lah (already)

example.target: Haba ngi la poi, ka bas ka la lah mih.
example.gloss: When we arrived, the bus had already left.

items.note: la lah is only used when two past events need ordering; otherwise plain la does. dep (finished) after the verb strengthens completion.

items.target: pronoun + dang + verb + naduh ___
items.gloss: present perfect continuous: present dang plus since

example.target: Ki dang trei ha kane ka kompani naduh 2015.
example.gloss: They have been working at this company since 2015.

items.note: The English tense collapses into present progressive plus a starting point. Never add la here; la dang would mean 'was doing' and end the action.

items.target: patient as subject + la + verb (+ da agent) / ki + verb (impersonal they)
items.gloss: passive: subject switch, or impersonal ki (they)

example.target: Ka lynti ka la shna da ka sorkar. Ki die ïa ka kwai hangne.
example.gloss: The road was built by the government. Betel is sold here (they sell betel here).

items.note: Khasi has no passive morphology. Either the thing is subject with la plus verb, or an impersonal ki (they) keeps active order. da marks the agent.

items.target: Lada ___ (bare verb), ___ yn ___ (same as T-COND1)
items.gloss: second conditional: identical to the first; unreality from context

example.target: Lada nga don kham bun ka por, ngan leit sha Sohra man ka taiew.
example.gloss: If I had more time, I'd go to Sohra every week.

items.note: There is no subjunctive or conditional form. Adverbs like shisha (really) or lehse (perhaps) tune how real the condition is.

items.target: u la ong ba + clause with original tense particles; pronouns shift
items.gloss: reported speech: no tense shift

example.target: U la ong ba u dang pang bad ba un ym wan.
example.gloss: He said he was ill and that he wouldn't come.

items.note: Keep the tense the speaker used: dang stays dang, yn stays yn. Only pronouns and words like mynta (now) or lashai change with the viewpoint.

items.target: wat la ___, ___ / la ___ ruh, ___
items.gloss: although ___, ___ / even though ___, ___

example.target: Wat la ka slap, ngi la leit sha Mawsmai.
example.gloss: Although it rained, we went to Mawsmai.

items.note: wat la opens the concession clause; the main clause follows in normal order. ruh at the end of the wat la clause strengthens it to 'even though'.

items.target: katba ___ (time) / hynrei ___ (contrast)
items.gloss: while ___ / whereas ___

example.target: Katba nga dang shet ja, u la sait ki plet; nga ieid ka sha hynrei u ieid ka kophi.
example.gloss: While I was cooking, he washed the plates; I like tea whereas he likes coffee.

items.note: katba is 'while, as long as' in time; for pure contrast Khasi just uses hynrei. Don't use katba for 'whereas'.

items.target: naba ___ / namar ba ___
items.gloss: since ___ / as ___ (reason)

example.target: Naba ka bas ka la lait, ngi la shim ka taxi.
example.gloss: Since the bus was late, we took a taxi.

items.note: naba is the reason 'since' and sounds slightly more written; namar ba is the everyday one. Neither means time-since, which is naduh.

items.target: khnang ba ___ / ba ___ yn ___
items.gloss: so that ___

example.target: Nga kren suki khnang ba phi lah ban sngewthuh.
example.gloss: I speak slowly so that you can understand.

items.note: khnang ba introduces a purpose clause with its own subject. When the subject is the same, drop to ban plus verb (G-IN-ORDER-TO).

items.target: ban ___ / khnang ban ___
items.gloss: to ___ / in order to ___

example.target: Nga la wan sha Shillong ban nang ka ktien Khasi.
example.gloss: I came to Shillong to learn Khasi.

items.note: ban plus verb after a motion or action verb is purpose; khnang ban makes it explicit and formal. Never use sha (to a place) for purpose.

items.target: ha kaba ___ (where) / ka por ba ___ (when) / ba ka ___ jong u (whose)
items.gloss: the place where ___ / the time when ___ / the man whose ___

example.target: Kane ka dei ka shnong ha kaba nga la kha, bad u briew ba ka ïing jong u ka la duh.
example.gloss: This is the village where I was born, and the man whose house burned down.

items.note: 'Where' is ha kaba (in which); 'whose' has no word, so Khasi says ba plus the noun with jong u/ka inside the clause. Keep the marker matching the head noun.

items.target: ap ïa (wait for), pyrkhat shaphang (think about), ïadei bad (depend on, relate to), kren shaphang (talk about), wad ïa (look for), peit ïa (look at), pan ïa (ask for), ai ïa (give to), sngap ïa (listen to), kynmaw ïa (remember)
items.gloss: wait for, think about, depend on, talk about, look for, look at, ask for, give to, listen to, remember

example.target: Nga dang ap ïa ka bas; nga dang pyrkhat shaphang ka kam; kata ka ïadei bad ka dor.
example.gloss: I'm waiting for the bus; I'm thinking about work; that depends on the price.

items.note: Most English verb-plus-preposition pairs are simply verb plus ïa in Khasi; shaphang is the odd one out for topics. Don't add sha or ha where ïa does the job.

items.target: lane ___ lane ___ / ym ___, ym ___ ruh
items.gloss: either ___ or ___ / neither ___ nor ___

example.target: Lane ka sha lane ka kophi, kaei kaei ruh bha. Ngam kwah ka doh, ngam kwah ka dohkha ruh.
example.gloss: Either tea or coffee, either is fine. I want neither meat nor fish.

items.note: lane repeated gives either/or. Neither/nor is two negatives with ruh (also) on the second; Khasi has no single 'neither' word.

items.target: tang ynda ___ / haduh ba ___ (by the time)
items.gloss: as soon as ___ / by the time ___

example.target: Tang ynda nga poi ha ïing, ngan phone ïa phi.
example.gloss: As soon as I get home, I'll phone you.

items.note: ynda (once, after) plus tang (only, just) is 'as soon as'. haduh ba is 'by the time'. The main clause takes yn for the future.

items.target: ha jaka ban ___ / khlem ___ (without) / ym tang ___ (apart from)
items.gloss: instead of ___ / without ___ / apart from ___

example.target: Ha jaka ban shim ka taxi, ngi la ïaid. Khlem ka syrbaïn phim lah ban leit.
example.gloss: Instead of taking a taxi, we walked. Without an umbrella you can't go.

items.note: ha jaka ban (in place of doing) is formal; speech usually says ym ... hynrei (not X but Y). khlem is 'without' and also 'not having done'.

items.target: uba / kaba / iba / kiba (subject or object); ïa uba (whom); jong uba (whose); ha kaba (where)
items.gloss: relative markers in all roles

example.target: Ka kynthei kaba nga la ïohi ka dei ka nonghikai ba ka khun jong ka ka pule bad nga.
example.gloss: The woman I saw is the teacher whose daughter studies with me.

items.note: One form uba/kaba serves subject and object; the gap tells you which. For whose, Khasi restates the possessor inside the clause with jong u/ka.

items.target: ïalade (oneself, object) / ___ hi (myself, emphatic) / ïa- prefix (each other)
items.gloss: reflexive and reciprocal

example.target: Nga la leh ïalade; nga hi nga la thoh kane; ki ïaieid.
example.gloss: I hurt myself; I myself wrote this; they love each other.

items.note: ïalade is the same for every person. hi after a pronoun is emphatic 'myself'. The prefix ïa- makes reciprocals: ïakynduh (meet), ïakren (converse), ïaleh (fight).

items.target: khyndiat (a bit), katto katne (a few), bha (quite), kham (rather, more), suki (hardly, slowly), tang (only)
items.gloss: a few, a bit, quite, rather, hardly

example.target: Nga tip khyndiat ka Khasi; ka jingbam ka bha shibun; tang katto katne ki briew ki la wan.
example.gloss: I know a bit of Khasi; the food is quite good; only a few people came.

items.note: Most quantity adverbs follow the word they modify (bha shibun), but tang (only) and katto katne precede. 'Hardly' is usually a negative plus khyndiat.

items.target: adjective + tam (the most) / kham ___ tam / ___ kat ___ (as ... as)
items.gloss: superlative with tam; equality with kat

example.target: Ka Sohra ka long ka jaka ba slap tam ha ka pyrthei; u jrong kat u kpa jong u.
example.gloss: Sohra is the rainiest place in the world; he is as tall as his father.

items.note: tam after the adjective is the superlative; kham ... tam is emphatic. 'As X as' is adjective plus kat plus the standard, or kat kum for comparisons of manner.

items.target: ka ___ jong ka ___ / u ___ jong u ___ (of); noun + noun (compound)
items.gloss: possession between nouns

example.target: Ka jingkhang jong ka ïing; ka kali jong u Bah; ka ïing skul.
example.gloss: The door of the house; Bah's car; the school building.

items.note: Possessed noun first, then jong, then the possessor with its marker. Fixed compounds drop jong: ka ïing skul, u khun ksew (puppy).

items.target: ka jingmut (opinion, meaning), ka jingpyrkhat (thought), ka jingpeit (view), ka daw (reason), u nuksa (example), ka jingshisha (truth), ka khubor (news), ka kot khubor (newspaper), ka TV (TV), ka jingïakren (discussion), ïakren (discuss), mynjur (agree), ngeit (believe), pyrkhat (think), ka jingsngewthuh (understanding), ka jingkylli (question)
items.gloss: Opinion, argument, media
items.note: Nouns from verbs take jing-: pyrkhat / ka jingpyrkhat, kren / ka jingkren. Shillong's Khasi papers (U Mawphor, U Nongsain Hima) are the reading practice.

items.target: sngewkmen (happy), sngewsih (sad, sorry), sngewbha (pleased), ieid (love), ka jingieid (love), sheptieng (afraid), ka jingsheptieng (fear), bitar (angry), sngewrem (ashamed), thngan (hungry), sliang (thirsty), sngewtynnad (enjoy), ngeit (trust), u/ka lok (friend), poikha (marry), ka jingïadei (relationship)
items.gloss: Feelings and relationships
items.note: Most feelings begin with sngew- (feel): sngewkmen, sngewsih, sngewbha. They are verbs, so no 'be': nga sngewkmen (I'm happy), nga la sngewsih (I was sad).

items.target: ka mariang (nature), ka khlaw (forest), ka dieng (tree), ka wah (river), ka lum (hill), ka lyngkha (field), ka pyrthei (world, earth), ka bneng (sky), ka shnong (village, town), ka nongbah (city), ka lynti (road), ka um (water), ka khyndew (soil, land), ka jingjakhlia (dirt, pollution), pynjakhlia (pollute), ka jingpyrshang ban da ki mariang (conservation effort)
items.gloss: Environment, city, nature
items.note: Meghalaya's sacred groves are ki law kyntang; khlaw is the ordinary forest. Shillong is simply ka nongbah (the city) in conversation.

items.target: ka skul (school), ka kolej (college), ka university (university), pule (study, read), nang (learn), hikai (teach), u/ka nonghikai (teacher), u/ka nongpule (student), ka jingnang (learning), ka jingtip (knowledge), ka kot (book), ka klas (class), ka exam (exam), pass (pass), ka kam (career), ka jingpule (studies)
items.gloss: Education, learning, career
items.note: pule is read and study at once; nang is learn as a skill or habit. English school words (klas, exam, degree) are used as loans by everyone.

items.target: ka ïing (house), ka kamra (room), ka jingkhang (door), ka jaka (place, plot), shong (live, stay), ka jingshong (dwelling), u/ka trai ïing (landlord, house owner), ka dor ka ïing (rent), ki para shnong (neighbours, fellow villagers), ka shnong (locality), ka ïing thymmai (new house), ka ïing tymmen (old house), ka um (water supply), ka ding (electricity, fire), ka lynti (road), ka jingkhreh (repair)
items.gloss: Housing, renting, neighbours
items.note: trai is owner: u trai ïing is the landlord. Rent is asked as katno ka dor ka ïing man u bnai? (what is the house price per month?).

items.target: ka phone (phone), ka mobile (mobile), ka komputer (computer), ka internet (internet), ka email (email), ka mesej (message), phah (send), ïoh (receive, get), ka dur (picture, photo), ka video (video), ka jingrwai (song, music), ka app (app), ka net (data, network), charge (charge), ka jingkhih (signal, movement), ka website (website)
items.gloss: Technology and the internet
items.note: Tech vocabulary is English inside Khasi grammar: phah ka email (send an email), ka net kam don (there's no network). dur is the native word for picture and photo.

items.target: pronoun plus yn or ym fuses (ngan, ngam, un, um, kan, kam, phin, phim); ïa shrinks to a glide; ban to bn
items.gloss: In fast speech the particles melt into the pronoun: nga ym becomes ngam, u yn becomes un, and these are how they are written too. ïa before a marker becomes a single syllable (ïa u sounds like yau). ban loses its vowel (kwah bn leit), and sngewbha comes out as ngewbha. Listen for the stressed final syllables and rebuild the grammar words around them.

items.target: the swallowed markers: la, ïa, ba, jong; dropped subject echoes; English loans with Khasi stress
items.gloss: At speed, la and ba are barely a flick of the tongue, and jong drops entirely (ka ïing nga). The subject echo (u Bah u wan) collapses to one u. English loans take final stress and Khasi vowels: ophis, kolej, bas STAND. The verb root is always clearly audible; if you catch the root and the pronoun you have the sentence.

items.target: Ha ka jingpeit jong nga, ___ / Nga pyrkhat ba ___
items.gloss: In my view, ___ / I think that ___

example.target: Ha ka jingpeit jong nga, ka Sohra ka kham bha ban ïa ka Shillong ban shong.
example.gloss: In my view, Sohra is better than Shillong to live in.

items.note: jingpeit (view, from peit, look) and jingmut (opinion) both work. The phrase is fronted and followed by a normal clause; no comma intonation is needed.

items.target: Nga mynjur / Shisha hi / Phi dei
items.gloss: I agree / Exactly (true indeed) / You're right

example.target: Ka jingtrei na ïing ka bha. — Shisha hi, nga mynjur bad phi.
example.gloss: Working from home is good. — Exactly, I agree with you.

items.note: mynjur is agree, consent; shisha hi is 'truly indeed'; phi dei is 'you are right' because dei means correct. Add bad phi (with you) after mynjur.

items.target: Nga sngewthuh ïa phi, hynrei ___
items.gloss: I understand you, but ___

example.target: Nga sngewthuh ïa phi, hynrei ngam pyrkhat ba kan trei.
example.gloss: I see your point, but I don't think it will work.

items.note: sngewthuh ïa (understand someone) is the concession; hynrei carries the turn. ka trei (it works) is used for plans as well as machines.

items.target: Ka daw ka long ba ___ / Ka kam ka long kumne: ___
items.gloss: The reason is that ___ / The matter is like this: ___

example.target: Ka daw ka long ba ka kamra ka ïalam shibun bad ka wifi kam trei.
example.gloss: The thing is, the room is very noisy and the wifi doesn't work.

items.note: daw is reason; ka daw ka long ba is the everyday launch of an explanation. kumne (like this) introduces a list of problems.

items.target: Phi pyrkhat kumno? / Kumno phi pyrkhat?
items.gloss: What do you think? / How do you think?

example.target: Ngan shim kane ka kam ne em? Phi pyrkhat kumno?
example.gloss: Shall I take this job or not? What do you think?

items.note: Khasi asks 'how do you think', not 'what'; aiu would be wrong here. Both orders are fine; the version with kumno last rises more.

items.target: Lada nga long phi, ngan ___ / Lada nga long ha ka jaka jong phi, ___
items.gloss: If I were you, I'd ___ / If I were in your place, I'd ___

example.target: Lada nga long phi, ngan kren bad u bah shwa.
example.gloss: If I were you, I'd talk to the boss first.

items.note: long phi is literally 'be you'; the longer ha ka jaka jong phi (in your place) is more natural for elders. Main clause takes plain yn (ngan).

items.target: Ban kren shisha, ___ / Ban ong shisha, ___
items.gloss: To speak truly, ___ / To say truly, ___

example.target: Ban kren shisha, ngam ieid ïa kane ka jingpyrkhat.
example.gloss: To be honest, I don't like this idea.

items.note: ban plus verb plus shisha (truly) is the fronted hedge. shisha also stands alone as 'really?' with rising tone.

items.target: Ka ïadei (bad ___) / Ka long ha ___
items.gloss: It depends (on ___) / It lies with ___

example.target: Phin wan ne em? — Ka ïadei bad ka por trei jong nga.
example.gloss: Will you come or not? — It depends on my work hours.

items.note: ïadei is 'be related, concern'; with bad it means 'depends on'. Ka long ha phi (it lies with you) is 'it's up to you'.

items.target: Ka daw ba nyngkong, ___; ba ar, ___ / Shisha hi ba ___, hynrei ___
items.gloss: First, ___; second, ___ / It is true that ___, but ___

example.target: Ka daw ba nyngkong, ki nongtrei ki sngewkmen kham bun; ba ar, ka kam ka kham bha.
example.gloss: First, workers are happier; second, the work is better.

items.note: Uses G-SEQUENCE, C-ADMITTEDLY, G-HOWEVER, D-IF-I-WERE. Points are numbered with ba nyngkong, ba ar, ba lai; the concession is shisha hi ... hynrei.

items.target: Lehse ___ / Nga pyrkhat ba lehse ___ / Kat ba nga tip, ___
items.gloss: Perhaps ___ / I think perhaps ___ / As far as I know, ___

example.target: Kat ba nga tip, lehse ka bas ka mih ha hynriew baje, hynrei ngam tip shisha.
example.gloss: As far as I know, the bus perhaps leaves at six, but I'm not sure.
